Introduction

Hypertension (BP ≥130/80 mmHg per ACC/AHA 2017; ≥140/90 mmHg per JNC 8 / WHO) is a major modifiable risk factor for cardiovascular disease, stroke, and renal failure. Pharmacotherapy is indicated when lifestyle modifications fail to control BP or when target organ damage is present.

Classification of Antihypertensive Drugs (5 marks)

A. Diuretics

  • Thiazides & thiazide-like — Hydrochlorothiazide, Chlorthalidone (most effective, longer acting), Indapamide, Metolazone.
  • Loop diuretics — Furosemide, Torsemide, Bumetanide, Ethacrynic acid.
  • Potassium-sparing — Spironolactone, Eplerenone, Amiloride, Triamterene.

B. Drugs Affecting the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS)

  • ACE inhibitors (ACEIs) — Enalapril, Lisinopril, Ramipril, Perindopril, Captopril, Fosinopril.
  • Angiotensin Receptor Blockers (ARBs / Sartans) — Losartan, Valsartan, Telmisartan, Olmesartan, Irbesartan, Candesartan.
  • Direct Renin Inhibitors — Aliskiren.
  • Aldosterone Antagonists (Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists) — Spironolactone, Eplerenone.

C. Calcium Channel Blockers (CCBs)

  • Dihydropyridines (DHP) — Amlodipine, Nifedipine, Felodipine, Nicardipine, Nitrendipine, Lercanidipine, Clevidipine.
  • Non-dihydropyridines (Non-DHP):
    • Phenylalkylamines — Verapamil.
    • Benzothiazepines — Diltiazem.

D. Sympatholytics (Drugs Affecting Sympathetic Nervous System)

  • β-Adrenergic Blockers (β-Blockers):
    • Non-selective (β1 + β2) — Propranolol, Timolol, Nadolol, Sotalol.
    • Cardioselective (β1) — Atenolol, Metoprolol, Bisoprolol, Nebivolol (also NO-mediated vasodilation), Betaxolol, Acebutolol.
    • Non-selective with α-blockade — Carvedilol, Labetalol.
    • With intrinsic sympathomimetic activity (ISA) — Pindolol, Acebutolol.
  • α-Adrenergic Blockers (α-Blockers):
    • Non-selective (α1 + α2) — Phenoxybenzamine (irreversible), Phentolamine (reversible).
    • Selective α1-blockers — Prazosin, Terazosin, Doxazosin, Tamsulosin (uroselective), Silodosin.
  • Centrally Acting Sympatholytics (α2-Agonists) — Clonidine, Methyldopa, Guanfacine, Guanabenz, α-Methyl DOPA.
  • Adrenergic Neuron Blockers — Reserpine, Guanethidine (historical; rarely used).

E. Vasodilators

  • Direct (Arterial) Vasodilators — Hydralazine, Minoxidil, Sodium nitroprusside (arterial + venous), Diazoxide.
  • Potassium Channel Openers — Minoxidil, Diazoxide, Nicorandil.
  • Nitrovasodilators — Sodium nitroprusside, Nitroglycerin.

F. Newer/Emerging Agents

  • Endothelin Receptor Antagonists — Bosentan, Ambrisentan ( pulmonary hypertension).
  • Neprilysin Inhibitor + ARB (ARNI) — Sacubitril/Valsartan (heart failure).
  • Dopamine β-hydroxylase Inhibitors — Nepicastat (investigational).
  • Vasopeptidase Inhibitors — Omapatrilat (failed trials).

G. Fixed-Dose Combinations (FDCs)

  • ACEI/ARB + Thiazide — e.g., Losartan + Hydrochlorothiazide, Ramipril + Hydrochlorothiazide.
  • ACEI + CCB — e.g., Amlodipine + Lisinopril, Perindopril + Amlodipine.
  • ARB + CCB — e.g., Valsartan + Amlodipine, Telmisartan + Amlodipine.
  • Triple combination — ACEI/ARB + CCB + Thiazide.

ACE Inhibitors (5 marks)

Mechanism of Action

  1. Inhibition of Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme (ACE / Kininase II):
    • ACE converts Angiotensin I → Angiotensin II (potent vasoconstrictor, aldosterone stimulant, sympathetic activator, growth promoter).
    • ACE also degrades bradykinin (vasodilator) — ACE inhibition → ↑bradykinin → ↑NO, prostacyclin → additional vasodilation.
  2. Reduced Angiotensin II:
    • Decreased vasoconstriction (arterial & venous) → ↓ peripheral resistance.
    • Decreased aldosterone secretion → ↓ sodium & water retention → ↓ blood volume.
    • Decreased sympathetic outflow (↓ noradrenaline release).
    • Decreased ADH release.
    • Reduced vascular & cardiac remodelling (↓ hypertrophy, ↓ fibrosis).
    • Reduced renal efferent arteriolar resistance → ↓ intraglomerular pressure → renal protection in diabetes & chronic kidney disease.
  3. Increased Bradykinin — contributes to vasodilation; also responsible for side effects (cough, angioedema).

Pharmacokinetics

  • Most are prodrugs (enalapril → enalaprilat; ramipril → ramiprilat) — except captopril & lisinopril (active).
  • Oral; well absorbed; hepatic conversion for prodrugs; renal excretion (except fosinopril — hepatic & renal).
  • Half-life varies — captopril (short, 2 h, TID); enalapril, ramipril (long, once daily).
  • Onset — 1 h (captopril); 4–6 h (others); peak 3–4 h.

Therapeutic Uses

  1. Hypertension — first-line; especially in diabetes, chronic kidney disease, heart failure, post-MI.
  2. Heart failure (systolic) — reduce mortality (CONSENSUS, SOLVD trials); cornerstone of therapy with β-blockers.
  3. Post-myocardial infarction — reduce remodelling, mortality (SAVE, AIRE, TRACE trials).
  4. Diabetic nephropathy — renal protection; reduce proteinuria, slow progression to ESRD.
  5. Non-diabetic chronic kidney disease — slow progression if proteinuria present.
  6. High cardiovascular risk — prevention (HOPE trial — ramipril reduced CV events in high-risk patients without hypertension or heart failure).
  7. Scleroderma renal crisis — ACE inhibitor is treatment of choice.
  8. Migraine prophylaxis — some evidence.

Adverse Effects

  • Dry cough — 5–20%; due to ↑bradykinin & substance P in lungs; switching to ARB usually resolves.
  • Angioedema — rare (0.1–0.7%) but life-threatening; due to ↑bradykinin; more common in Black patients; swelling of face, lips, tongue, larynx — airway obstruction. Stop ACEI immediately; treat with epinephrine, antihistamines, corticosteroids, icatibant (bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist), C1 esterase inhibitor concentrate. Never rechallenge.
  • Hypotension — first-dose effect (especially with diuretics, sodium depletion); start low, titrate.
  • Hyperkalaemia — ↓aldosterone → potassium retention; monitor K⁺; avoid potassium supplements, potassium-sparing diuretics, salt substitutes.
  • Acute kidney injury — especially in bilateral renal artery stenosis (↓efferent arteriolar tone → ↓GFR); volume depletion; NSAIDs.
  • Renal impairment in bilateral renal artery stenosis — contraindication; ACEI dilates efferent arteriole → ↓GFR → AKI.
  • Foetal toxicity — teratogenic (contraindicated in pregnancy, especially 2nd & 3rd trimester); causes renal agenesis, oligohydramnios, pulmonary hypoplasia, limb contractures, hypocalvaria (Pallister-Hall-like syndrome — "ACE inhibitor foetopathy").
  • Skin rash — maculopapular; more common with captopril (sulphydryl group).
  • Loss of taste (dysgeusia) — captopril-specific (sulphydryl group).
  • Proteinuria — rare; usually in pre-existing renal disease.
  • Neutropenia — rare; in patients with collagen vascular disease, renal impairment (captopril).

Contraindications

  • Pregnancy (teratogenic).
  • Bilateral renal artery stenosis.
  • History of angioedema.
  • Hyperkalaemia.
  • Severe aortic stenosis, hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM).
  • Caution — hypovolaemia, hyponatraemia, severe renal impairment, elderly.

Precautions

  • Monitor — BP, renal function (creatinine, urea), electrolytes (K⁺, Na⁺) at baseline & 1–2 weeks after starting or dose increase.
  • Avoid NSAIDs (↓antihypertensive effect, ↑renal risk).
  • Avoid potassium supplements, potassium-sparing diuretics.
  • Caution in elderly, volume-depleted, renal impairment.

Choice of Antihypertensive — JNC 8 / ACC-AHA Guidelines (2 marks)

  • First-line (general population) — Thiazide diuretic, ACEI/ARB, CCB (any one or combination).
  • Diabetes — ACEI or ARB (renal protection); add thiazide or CCB if needed.
  • Chronic kidney disease with proteinuria — ACEI or ARB (renal protection).
  • Heart failure — ACEI/ARB + β-blocker + aldosterone antagonist + diuretic; avoid CCB (non-DHP).
  • Post-MI — β-blocker + ACEI + ARB (if ACEI intolerant) + aldosterone antagonist.
  • Black patients — thiazide or CCB preferred first-line (less response to ACEI monotherapy); ACEI if heart failure or CKD.
  • Elderly isolated systolic hypertension — thiazide or DHP-CCB (SHEP, Syst-Eur trials).
  • Benign prostatic hyperplasia — α1-blocker (doxazosin, tamsulosin).
  • Pregnancy — Methyldopa, Labetalol, Nifedipine; avoid ACEI, ARB, direct renin inhibitor, nitroprusside.
  • Angina — β-blocker + CCB.
  • Atrial fibrillation — ARB or ACEI (reduce recurrence, prevent remodelling).
  • Gout — avoid thiazides (raise uric acid); use losartan (mild uricosuric).
  • Asthma/COPD — avoid β-blockers (non-selective); cardioselective may be used cautiously.
  • Stroke prevention — ACEI + thiazide (PROGRESS trial — perindopril + indapamide reduced stroke recurrence).

Combination Therapy (3 marks)

Most patients need ≥2 drugs to achieve target BP (<130/80 or <140/90). Complementary mechanisms:

  • ACEI + Thiazide — synergistic; thiazide activates RAAS (counteracted by ACEI); prevents hypokalaemia.
  • ACEI + CCB — most effective combination (ACCOMPLISH trial — superior to ACEI + thiazide); well-tolerated; metabolic neutral.
  • ARB + CCB — alternative to ACEI + CCB (cough/angioedema intolerance).
  • β-blocker + diuretic — historical; less favourable metabolic profile.
  • Avoid:
    • ACEI + ARB (↑hyperkalaemia, AKI, no added benefit — ONTARGET trial).
    • ACEI + direct renin inhibitor (aliskiren) — similar concern.
    • Non-DHP CCB (verapamil/diltiazem) + β-blocker (bradycardia, AV block).

Treatment Approach

  1. Stage 1 hypertension (130–139/80–89 mmHg) — lifestyle modification 3–6 months; add drug if target organ damage or CV risk ≥10%.
  2. Stage 2 hypertension (≥140/90 mmHg) — start 2 drugs (ACEI/ARB + thiazide or CCB).
  3. Resistant hypertension — BP uncontrolled on 3 drugs (including diuretic) at full doses; add spironolactone (PATHWAY-2 trial), α-blocker, β-blocker, or refer for renal denervation.
  4. Hypertensive emergency — IV labetalol, nitroprusside, nicardipine, fenoldopam, clevidipine, esmolol.
  5. Hypertensive urgency — oral captopril, clonidine, labetalol, amlodipine; gradual reduction over 24–48 h.

Clinical Pearl

ACE inhibitors (ending in "-pril") and ARBs (ending in "-sartan") are first-line antihypertensives in diabetes & chronic kidney disease — they reduce proteinuria & slow progression to ESRD by lowering intraglomerular pressure (dilating efferent arteriole). The dry cough (5–20%) is due to bradykinin accumulation — switch to ARB. Angioedema (0.1–0.7%) is life-threatening — more common in Black patients; never rechallenge; treat with epinephrine, icatibant (bradykinin B2 antagonist). ACEI + CCB is the most effective 2-drug combination (ACCOMPLISH trial) — superior to ACEI + thiazide. Never combine ACEI + ARB — increases hyperkalaemia & AKI without added benefit (ONTARGET trial). ACEI are teratogenic — contraindicated in pregnancy (use methyldopa, labetalol, nifedipine). Always monitor renal function & potassium 1–2 weeks after starting or dose increase — small rise in creatinine (up to 30%) is acceptable; larger rise suggests renal artery stenosis or volume depletion. The HOPE trial (ramipril in high-risk patients without hypertension) showed ACEI reduces CV events beyond BP lowering — vasculoprotective effect. India — hypertension is the leading cause of mortality & disability; prevalence ~25% in adults; control rates poor (<20%); salt reduction, lifestyle modification, & affordable generic antihypertensives (amlodipine, atenolol, hydrochlorothiazide, ramipril) are keys to population-level control.

Definition of Bioavailability (2 marks)

Bioavailability is defined as the fraction or percentage of an administered dose of a drug that reaches the systemic circulation in an unchanged (active) form, and the rate at which this occurs. It is a measure of both the extent (amount) and rate (speed) of drug absorption.

  • For intravenous (IV) administration — bioavailability is 100% (or 1.0) by definition, because the entire dose enters systemic circulation directly.
  • For other routes (oral, intramuscular, subcutaneous, sublingual, rectal, topical) — bioavailability is generally <100% due to incomplete absorption and/or first-pass metabolism.
  • Bioavailability is denoted by F (fraction absorbed); values range from 0 to 1 (or 0% to 100%).
  • Mathematically: F = (AUC oral / AUC IV) × (Dose IV / Dose oral), where AUC = area under the plasma concentration-time curve.

Importance of Bioavailability

  • Determines the dose needed for non-IV routes (e.g., if oral F = 0.5, oral dose = 2 × IV dose for equivalent effect).
  • Affects onset, duration, and intensity of drug action.
  • Explains interindividual variability in drug response.
  • Influences dosage form design & drug development.
  • Bioequivalence studies — compare generic vs branded formulations (FDA requires 80–125% confidence interval for AUC & Cmax).

Factors Affecting Bioavailability (8 marks)

A. Physicochemical Properties of the Drug

  1. Lipid solubility / partition coefficient:
    • Drugs cross biological membranes (lipid bilayers) by passive diffusion — only lipid-soluble (non-ionised) forms cross readily.
    • Higher lipid solubility → better absorption → higher bioavailability.
    • Example — lipid-soluble drugs (diazepam, propranolol) are well absorbed; lipid-insoluble drugs (atropine, neostigmine) are poorly absorbed.
  2. Ionisation (pKa) & pH:
    • Henderson-Hasselbalch equation: for weak acid — pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]); for weak base — pH = pKa + log([B]/[BH⁺]).
    • Weak acids are better absorbed in acidic environment (stomach) — non-ionised form predominates (e.g., aspirin, barbiturates).
    • Weak bases are better absorbed in alkaline environment (intestine) — non-ionised form predominates (e.g., diazepam, amphetamine).
    • pH-partition hypothesis — non-ionised (lipid-soluble) form crosses membranes; ionised form does not.
    • Most drugs are absorbed in small intestine (huge surface area, alkaline pH, long transit time) — not stomach.
  3. Molecular size/weight:
    • Smaller molecules (MW <500 Da) cross membranes more easily.
    • Large molecules (proteins, peptides — insulin, heparin) are poorly absorbed orally — must be given parenterally.
  4. Chemical stability:
    • Drugs degraded by gastric acid (penicillin G, insulin, erythromycin) have low oral bioavailability.
    • Enteric-coated formulations protect acid-labile drugs.
  5. Dosage form:
    • Solutions > suspensions > capsules > tablets > coated tablets (rate of dissolution).
    • Modified-release formulations (sustained, extended, delayed) have slower absorption.
    • Particle size, polymorphism, salt form affect dissolution (Noyes-Whitney equation).
  6. Dissolution rate (Noyes-Whitney equation):
    • dC/dt = (D × S / h) × (Cs - C)
    • D = diffusion coefficient; S = surface area; h = thickness of diffusion layer; Cs = saturation solubility; C = concentration in bulk.
    • ↑Surface area (smaller particles), ↑solubility, ↓diffusion layer thickness → ↑dissolution → ↑bioavailability.

B. Physiological Factors

  1. Gastric emptying time:
    • Faster gastric emptying → faster absorption (drug reaches small intestine sooner).
    • Delayed by — food (especially fatty), opioids, anticholinergics, tricyclics, pregnancy, diabetic gastroparesis.
    • Sped up by — metoclopramide, domperidone, erythromycin (motilin agonist), fasting.
    • Drugs absorbed in stomach (weak acids — aspirin) — delayed gastric emptying may increase absorption; drugs absorbed in intestine — delayed emptying delays absorption.
  2. Intestinal motility & transit time:
    • Most drugs absorbed in small intestine (large surface area — villi & microvilli).
    • Increased motility → ↓ contact time → ↓ absorption (e.g., diarrhoea).
    • Decreased motility → ↑ contact time → ↑ absorption (e.g., opioids, anticholinergics).
  3. pH of gastrointestinal tract:
    • Stomach pH 1–3; intestine pH 5–7; colon pH 7–8.
    • Achlorhydria (pernicious anaemia, elderly, PPIs) — ↑ pH → ↓ absorption of weak acids, ↑ absorption of weak bases.
    • H2 blockers, PPIs — ↑ gastric pH; affect absorption of ketoconazole, itraconazole, atazanavir (need acid).
  4. Surface area:
    • Small intestine has largest surface area (villi, microvilli) — primary site of absorption.
    • Disease states (Crohn's, coeliac, short bowel syndrome) reduce surface area → ↓ absorption.
  5. Blood flow to GIT:
    • Splanchnic blood flow (200–500 mL/min) — absorbs drugs rapidly; equilibrates with systemic circulation.
    • Reduced in congestive heart failure, shock → ↓ absorption.
  6. Presence of food:
    • May delay gastric emptying, alter pH, bind drug, or affect dissolution.
    • ↑Absorption — griseofulvin, diazepam, propranolol, phenytoin (with food).
    • ↓Absorption — tetracyclines (with dairy — Ca²⁺ chelation); penicillins, cephalosporins, levodopa (with protein); iron (with tea — tannins).
    • Food-drug interactions — grapefruit juice (CYP3A4 inhibition → ↑ bioavailability of statins, CCBs, cyclosporine, tacrolimus, midazolam).
  7. Presence of other drugs (drug-drug interactions):
    • Chelation — tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones + Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, Fe²⁺, Al³⁺, Zn²⁺ (antacids, dairy, iron supplements) → ↓ absorption.
    • Adsorption — activated charcoal, cholestyramine, kaolin → ↓ absorption of co-administered drugs.
    • Altered gut flora — antibiotics ↓ bacterial deconjugation of oestrogen contraceptives → ↓ efficacy.
    • Altered gastric pH — PPIs, H2 blockers affect absorption of acid-dependent drugs (ketoconazole, atazanavir).
    • Altered motility — metoclopramide speeds absorption; anticholinergics delay.
  8. GI enzymes & transporters:
    • P-glycoprotein (P-gp, MDR1) efflux pump — present in enterocytes; pumps drugs back into intestinal lumen → ↓ absorption (digoxin, cyclosporine, tacrolimus, many HIV protease inhibitors).
    • P-gp inhibitors — verapamil, quinidine, amiodarone, grapefruit juice → ↑ digoxin levels.
    • P-gp inducers — rifampin → ↓ digoxin levels.
    • OATP, PEPT1, other transporters — may facilitate or inhibit absorption.
  9. Age:
    • Neonates & infants — immature hepatic metabolism, reduced gastric acid → variable absorption & first-pass.
    • Elderly — reduced gastric acid (achlorhydria), reduced gut motility, reduced splanchnic blood flow — may affect absorption.
  10. Disease states:
    • Coeliac disease, Crohn's, short bowel syndrome, gastrectomy, achlorhydria, malabsorption syndromes — ↓ absorption.
    • Congestive heart failure, shock — ↓ splanchnic blood flow → ↓ absorption.
    • Liver disease — ↓ first-pass metabolism → ↑ bioavailability (e.g., propranolol, labetalol, morphine).
  11. Circadian rhythm — time of day affects absorption (theophylline, antihypertensives).

C. First-Pass Metabolism (Presystemic Metabolism) — Major Factor

D. Route of Administration

TransdermalVariable (depends on drug & formulation)

First-Pass (Presystemic) Metabolism (5 marks)

Definition

First-pass metabolism (presystemic elimination) refers to the metabolism of a drug that occurs between its site of administration and its entry into the systemic circulation, before it reaches its site of action. Most significant for orally administered drugs.

Sites of First-Pass Metabolism

  1. Gastrointestinal epithelium (enterocytes):
    • Express drug-metabolising enzymes — CYP3A4 (major), CYP2C9, CYP2D6, esterases, sulfotransferases, glucuronosyltransferases.
    • May metabolise drugs before absorption into portal blood.
    • P-glycoprotein efflux pump also contributes — pumps drugs back to lumen.
  2. Liver (hepatocytes) — main site:
    • Drugs absorbed from GIT enter portal vein → liver → systemic circulation.
    • Hepatic extraction ratio (E) — fraction removed in one pass through liver.
    • High extraction drugs (E >0.7) — extensive first-pass; low oral bioavailability (propranolol, morphine, lidocaine, nitroglycerin, verapamil, salbutamol, isoprenaline).
    • Low extraction drugs (E <0.3) — minimal first-pass; high oral bioavailability (diazepam, phenytoin, theophylline, warfarin).
    • Bioavailability = (1 - E) × fraction absorbed.
  3. Lung (pulmonary first-pass):
    • Pulmonary endothelium expresses enzymes (CYP, esterases, MAO).
    • May metabolise drugs before reaching systemic arteries.
    • Significant for — 5-HT, noradrenaline, prostaglandins, some inhaled drugs.
  4. Portal vein (limited metabolism) — minor.

Clinical Significance

  • Dose adjustment — oral dose must be higher than IV dose (e.g., propranolol oral 40 mg ≈ IV 1 mg; morphine oral 30 mg ≈ IV 10 mg).
  • Route selection — drugs with extensive first-pass (nitroglycerin, lidocaine) are given by alternate routes (sublingual, IV, transdermal).
  • Interindividual variability — genetic polymorphisms in CYP enzymes cause variable first-pass; propranolol bioavailability varies 10-fold.
  • Liver disease — ↓ first-pass metabolism → ↑ bioavailability; risk of toxicity (e.g., propranolol, morphine, labetalol in cirrhosis).
  • Cardiac failure — ↓ hepatic blood flow → ↓ first-pass → ↑ bioavailability.
  • Drug interactions — enzyme inducers (rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, barbiturates) ↑ first-pass → ↓ bioavailability; enzyme inhibitors (ketoconazole, erythromycin, grapefruit juice) ↓ first-pass → ↑ bioavailability.
  • Food effects — grapefruit juice inhibits intestinal CYP3A4 → ↑ bioavailability of statins, CCBs, cyclosporine, midazolam, saquinavir; can cause toxicity.
  • First-pass bypass routes — sublingual (nitroglycerin, buprenorphine, fentanyl, lorazepam), buccal, rectal (partial — 50% bypass), IV/IM, transdermal (fentanyl, nitroglycerin, oestrogen), inhalation.
  • Prodrug strategy — some drugs are given as prodrugs that are activated by first-pass metabolism (en al ap ril → enalaprilat; enalapril is more bioavailable than active enalaprilat).

Measurement of Bioavailability

  • Plasma concentration-time curve (AUC):
    • Plot plasma drug concentration vs time after oral & IV administration.
    • Calculate AUC (area under curve) by trapezoidal rule.
    • F (bioavailability) = (AUC oral × Dose IV) / (AUC IV × Dose oral).
  • Urine excretion data — cumulative amount of unchanged drug excreted in urine.
  • Pharmacodynamic endpoints — for drugs without measurable plasma levels (e.g., warfarin INR).

Bioequivalence

  • Two formulations of the same drug are bioequivalent if their bioavailability (AUC, Cmax, Tmax) is similar within defined limits.
  • FDA/CDSCO criteria — 90% confidence interval of the ratio (test/reference) for AUC & Cmax should be within 80–125% (log-transformed data).
  • Required for approval of generic drugs; ensures therapeutic equivalence.
  • Failure — generic formulations of narrow therapeutic index drugs (warfarin, phenytoin, digoxin, levothyroxine, lithium, cyclosporine) need careful monitoring.

Clinical Pearl

The single most important factor reducing oral bioavailability is first-pass hepatic metabolism — drugs like nitroglycerin (<5% oral bioavailability) are given sublingually to bypass the liver. Propranolol has variable bioavailability (10-fold interindividual variation) due to genetic differences in hepatic extraction — same oral dose may produce very different plasma levels. Grapefruit juice inhibits intestinal CYP3A4 → ↑ bioavailability of statins (simvastatin, atorvastatin), CCBs (felodipine, amlodipine), cyclosporine, tacrolimus, midazolam — can cause toxicity; advise patients to avoid. Always check bioavailability when converting IV to oral dosing — e.g., morphine oral:IV ratio is 3:1 (accounting for both bioavailability & first-pass); metoprolol oral:IV ratio is 2.5:1. Bioequivalence studies ensure generics are therapeutically equivalent to branded drugs — FDA requires 80–125% confidence interval for AUC & Cmax; for narrow therapeutic index drugs (warfarin, phenytoin, digoxin, levothyroxine), switching brands requires monitoring. P-glycoprotein efflux in enterocytes — important for digoxin, cyclosporine, tacrolimus; inhibitors (verapamil, quinidine, amiodarone, clarithromycin) ↑ levels; inducers (rifampin, St John's wort) ↓ levels. Prodrug strategy — enalapril (prodrug) is more bioavailable than active enalaprilat; levodopa is combined with carbidopa (peripheral DOPA decarboxylase inhibitor) to ↓ first-pass & ↑ brain delivery. Liver disease & cardiac failure — ↓ first-pass → ↑ bioavailability → risk of toxicity; reduce dose of high-extraction drugs (propranolol, morphine, labetalol, verapamil).

Definition of Receptors (2 marks)

A receptor is a specific cellular macromolecule (usually a protein) that binds a ligand (endogenous neurotransmitter, hormone, autacoid, or exogenous drug) and translates this binding into a cellular response — a change in cellular function. Receptors are the principal targets of drug action (~50% of all drugs act on receptors).

Properties of Receptors

  • Saturation — finite number of receptors; binding reaches a maximum.
  • Stereoselectivity — receptors recognise specific stereoisomers (e.g., L-noradrenaline >> D-noradrenaline; morphine (levorotatory) >> dextromethorphan (dextrorotatory)).
  • Specificity / selectivity — receptors bind only structurally related ligands.
  • Reversibility — binding is usually reversible (non-covalent) — except irreversible antagonists (phenoxybenzamine, aspirin on COX).
  • Agonist — binds & activates receptor; produces a response (e.g., adrenaline on β-receptor).
  • Antagonist — binds but does not activate; blocks agonist action (e.g., propranolol on β-receptor).
  • Partial agonist — binds & produces submaximal response; also blocks full agonist (e.g., pindolol, buprenorphine).
  • Inverse agonist — binds & reduces constitutive receptor activity (e.g., mirtazapine, some antihistamines).
  • Allosteric modulator — binds at a different site; enhances (positive) or inhibits (negative) agonist action (e.g., benzodiazepines on GABA-A; cinacalcet on calcium-sensing receptor).

Classification of Receptors (1 mark)

  1. Based on transduction mechanism (how the signal is converted to cellular response) — primary classification (discussed below).
  2. Based on localisation — cell surface (membrane) receptors; intracellular (cytoplasmic/nuclear) receptors.
  3. Based on ligand — neurotransmitter receptors (acetylcholine, noradrenaline, GABA, glutamate, dopamine, serotonin, opioid); hormone receptors (steroid, thyroid, peptide); autacoid receptors (histamine, prostaglandin, leukotriene, bradykinin, 5-HT); cytokine receptors; growth factor receptors.
  4. Based on structural homology — superfamilies (ligand-gated ion channels, GPCRs, kinase-linked, intracellular).

Classification Based on Transduction Mechanism (10 marks)

1. Ligand-Gated Ion Channels (Ionotropic Receptors, LGIC) — Fastest

  • Structure:
    • Multi-subunit transmembrane protein forming an ion channel.
    • Ligand binding site on extracellular face; channel pore in centre.
    • Usually pentameric (5 subunits) for Cys-loop superfamily; tetrameric for glutamate receptors.
  • Mechanism:
    1. Ligand binds → conformational change → channel opens.
    2. Ions flow down electrochemical gradient → change membrane potential → cellular response.
    3. Response is rapid (milliseconds) — suitable for fast synaptic transmission.
    4. Channels close when ligand dissociates; desensitisation with prolonged exposure.
  • Examples:
    • Nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR) — neuromuscular junction (NMJ), autonomic ganglia, CNS; Na⁺/K⁺/Ca²⁺ influx → depolarisation.
    • GABA-A receptor — CNS; Cl⁻ influx → hyperpolarisation → inhibition; target of benzodiazepines, barbiturates, alcohol, neurosteroids, general anaesthetics (propofol, etomidate).
    • Glycine receptor — spinal cord & brainstem; Cl⁻ influx → inhibition; blocked by strychnine (tetanus toxin).
    • Glutamate receptors (ionotropic):
      • NMDA — Ca²⁺ influx (voltage-dependent Mg²⁺ block); learning, memory, excitotoxicity; blocked by ketamine, memantine, magnesium.
      • AMPA — Na⁺ influx; fast excitatory transmission.
      • Kainate — Na⁺ influx; excitatory.
    • 5-HT3 receptor — CNS & periphery (vagus); Na⁺/K⁺ influx; nausea & vomiting; blocked by ondansetron, granisetron.
    • P2X (ATP) receptor — Na⁺/Ca²⁺ influx; pain, smooth muscle.
    • IP3 receptor, ryanodine receptor — intracellular Ca²⁺ channels (endoplasmic reticulum); Ca²⁺ release.
  • Drug targets — neuromuscular blockers (succinylcholine — depolarising; vecuronium, rocuronium — non-depolarising), benzodiazepines, barbiturates, ketamine, memantine, ondansetron.

2. G-Protein-Coupled Receptors (GPCRs, Metabotropic, 7-Transmembrane Receptors) — Largest Family

  • Structure:
    • Single polypeptide with 7 transmembrane α-helical domains (heptahelical).
    • Extracellular N-terminus (ligand binding); intracellular C-terminus (G-protein coupling).
    • Coupled to heterotrimeric G-proteins (α, β, γ subunits).
    • Largest receptor family — >800 in human genome; target of ~30% of all marketed drugs.
  • Mechanism:
    1. Ligand binds receptor → conformational change.
    2. Receptor activates G-protein (GDP → GTP exchange on α-subunit).
    3. α-subunit dissociates from βγ-dimer; both can regulate effectors.
    4. Effectors — adenylate cyclase (↑ or ↓ cAMP), phospholipase C (IP3, DAG), ion channels (K⁺, Ca²⁺), phosphodiesterase, RhoGEF.
    5. Second messengers (cAMP, cGMP, IP3, DAG, Ca²⁺) activate protein kinases (PKA, PKC, CaMK) → phosphorylation → cellular response.
    6. Response in seconds.
    7. GTP hydrolysis → G-protein reassociates → signal terminates; RGS (regulators of G-protein signalling) accelerate GTPase.
  • Classification by G-protein:
    • Gs (stimulatory) — ↑adenylyl cyclase → ↑cAMP → PKA. Examples — β1, β2, β3 adrenergic; D1, D5 dopamine; H2 histamine; glucagon; ACTH; TSH; LH; FSH; PTH; calcitonin; prostacyclin (IP).
    • Gi (inhibitory) — ↓adenylyl cyclase → ↓cAMP; opens K⁺ channels (hyperpolarisation); closes Ca²⁺ channels. Examples — α2 adrenergic; D2, D3, D4 dopamine; M2, M4 muscarinic; μ, δ, κ opioid; 5-HT1; GABA-B; somatostatin; adenosine A1; CB1, CB2 cannabinoid.
    • Gq — activates phospholipase C → IP3 (Ca²⁺ release) + DAG (PKC activation). Examples — α1 adrenergic; M1, M3, M5 muscarinic; H1 histamine; 5-HT2; B1, B2 bradykinin; vasopressin V1; angiotensin II AT1; endothelin ETA; thromboxane TP.
    • G12/13 — activates RhoGEF → RhoA → cytoskeletal changes, gene expression. Examples — thrombin, lysophosphatidic acid, sphingosine-1-phosphate.
  • Examples of GPCRs & drug targets:
    • Adrenergic receptors — α1 (prazosin — BPH, hypertension); α2 (clonidine — hypertension); β1 (atenolol — angina, hypertension); β2 (salbutamol — asthma); β3 (mirabegron — overactive bladder).
    • Muscarinic acetylcholine receptors (M1–M5) — atropine (non-selective); pirenzepine (M1); ipratropium (M3); oxybutynin (overactive bladder); pilocarpine (glaucoma).
    • Histamine receptors (H1, H2, H3, H4) — antihistamines (H1 — cetirizine, fexofenadine); H2 blockers (ranitidine — withdrawn; famotidine); H3 (pitolisant — narcolepsy).
    • Dopamine receptors (D1–D5) — antipsychotics (D2 blockade — haloperidol, risperidone); Parkinson's (D2 agonist — bromocriptine, ropinirole).
    • Serotonin (5-HT) receptors — 5-HT1A (buspirone, gepirone); 5-HT1B/D (triptans — sumatriptan); 5-HT2A (atypical antipsychotics, LSD); 5-HT3 (ondansetron); 5-HT4 (cisapride — withdrawn; tegaserod); 5-HT6, 5-HT7.
    • Opioid receptors (μ, δ, κ) — morphine, fentanyl, codeine, naloxone, buprenorphine, methadone.
    • Angiotensin II receptors (AT1, AT2) — losartan, valsartan, telmisartan (AT1 blockers).
    • Cannabinoid receptors (CB1, CB2) — rimonabant (CB1 inverse agonist — withdrawn); dronabinol, nabilone.
    • Chemokine receptors — maraviroc (CCR5 antagonist — HIV entry inhibitor).

3. Kinase-Linked Receptors (Enzyme-Linked, Catalytic Receptors)

  • Structure:
    • Single transmembrane polypeptide with extracellular ligand-binding domain & intracellular kinase domain (or associated kinase).
    • Most have tyrosine kinase activity (receptor tyrosine kinases, RTKs); some have serine/threonine kinase (TGF-β receptor) or guanylyl cyclase (ANP receptor).
    • Often dimerise on ligand binding.
  • Mechanism:
    1. Ligand binds → receptor dimerisation.
    2. Trans-autophosphorylation of tyrosine residues on intracellular domain.
    3. Phosphorylated tyrosines recruit signalling proteins (via SH2, SH3, PTB domains) — Grb2, SOS, Ras, Raf, MEK, ERK (MAPK pathway); PI3K-Akt-mTOR pathway; JAK-STAT pathway (cytokine receptors).
    4. Phosphorylation cascade → gene transcription → cellular response (growth, differentiation, survival, metabolism).
    5. Response in minutes to hours; long-lasting effects (gene expression).
    6. Termination — phosphatases (PTEN, SHP); receptor internalisation & degradation.
  • Examples:
    • Receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs):
      • Insulin receptor — insulin signalling; glucose uptake (GLUT4); glycogen, lipid, protein synthesis.
      • EGFR (ErbB1, HER1) — epithelial growth; cancers (NSCLC, colorectal); targeted by erlotinib, gefitinib, cetuximab, panitumumab.
      • HER2 (ErbB2) — breast cancer; trastuzumab (Herceptin), pertuzumab, lapatinib, T-DM1.
      • VEGFR (Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor Receptor) — angiogenesis; cancers; bevacizumab, sunitinib, sorafenib, pazopanib.
      • PDGFR (Platelet-Derived Growth Factor Receptor) — imatinib (Gleevec) — CML, GIST.
      • BCR-ABL — fusion protein in CML; imatinib, dasatinib, nilotinib.
      • c-KIT — GIST; imatinib.
      • FGFR (Fibroblast Growth Factor Receptor) — cancers; erdafitinib.
      • ALK — NSCLC; crizotinib, alectinib.
      • ROS1 — NSCLC; crizotinib.
      • JAK (Janus Kinase) — cytokine receptor-associated — tofacitinib, baricitinib, ruxolitinib (rheumatoid arthritis, myelofibrosis).
    • Serine/threonine kinase receptors:
      • TGF-β receptor — growth inhibition, fibrosis, immunosuppression; cancers (loss of function).
      • Bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) receptor.
    • Guanylyl cyclase-linked receptors:
      • ANP, BNP receptor (membrane) — natriuresis, vasodilation; sacubitril (neprilysin inhibitor) increases ANP.
      • Guanylate cyclase-C (GC-C) — intestinal; linaclotide, plecanatide (IBS-C, chronic constipation).
      • Soluble guanylyl cyclase (sGC) — NO receptor; riociguat (pulmonary hypertension).
    • Toll-like receptors (TLRs) — innate immunity; signal via MyD88, TRIF → NF-κB → cytokines.

4. Intracellular Receptors (Nuclear Receptors, Cytosolic Receptors) — Slowest

  • Structure:
    • Ligand-activated transcription factors located in cytoplasm or nucleus.
    • Single polypeptide with variable N-terminal domain, DNA-binding domain (zinc fingers), hinge, ligand-binding domain, C-terminal.
    • Bind lipophilic ligands (steroids, thyroid hormone, vitamin D, retinoic acid) that cross plasma membrane by diffusion.
  • Mechanism:
    1. Lipophilic ligand diffuses across plasma membrane.
    2. Binds intracellular receptor (cytoplasmic or nuclear).
    3. Conformational change → receptor dimerisation (homodimer or heterodimer with RXR).
    4. Receptor-ligand complex translocates to nucleus (if cytoplasmic); binds specific DNA sequences (hormone response elements — HRE).
    5. Recruits co-activators or co-repressors → modulates gene transcription.
    6. mRNA → protein synthesis → cellular response.
    7. Response in hours to days; long-lasting; affects protein synthesis.
  • Classification:
    • Type I (steroid receptors — cytoplasmic):
      • Glucocorticoid receptor (GR) — cortisol, prednisolone, dexamethasone; anti-inflammatory, immunosuppressive.
      • Mineralocorticoid receptor (MR) — aldosterone; spironolactone, eplerenone (antagonists); sodium retention, potassium excretion.
      • Androgen receptor (AR) — testosterone, dihydrotestosterone; prostate cancer; bicalutamide, enzalutamide, abiraterone.
      • Progesterone receptor (PR) — progesterone; medroxyprogesterone, megestrol; mifepristone (antagonist).
      • Oestrogen receptor (ER) — oestradiol; tamoxifen (SERM — partial antagonist in breast), raloxifene (SERM — agonist in bone, antagonist in breast & uterus), fulvestrant (pure antagonist), aromatase inhibitors (anastrozole, letrozole — reduce oestrogen synthesis).
    • Type II (non-steroid receptors — nuclear, heterodimerise with RXR):
      • Thyroid hormone receptor (TR) — T3, T4; metabolism, growth, development; levothyroxine.
      • Vitamin D receptor (VDR) — calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D); calcium homeostasis; calcitriol, paricalcitol.
      • Retinoic acid receptor (RAR) — all-trans retinoic acid; differentiation; tretinoin (APL treatment).
      • Retinoid X receptor (RXR) — 9-cis retinoic acid; heterodimer partner for TR, VDR, RAR, PPAR, LXR, FXR, PXR.
      • PPAR (peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor) — PPAR-α (fibrates — bezafibrate, fenofibrate; lipid metabolism); PPAR-γ (thiazolidinediones — pioglitazone, rosiglitazone; insulin sensitisation); PPAR-δ (investigational).
      • LXR (liver X receptor) — cholesterol homeostasis.
      • FXR (farnesoid X receptor) — bile acid homeostasis; obeticholic acid (PBC).
      • PXR (pregnane X receptor) — drug metabolism (CYP3A4 induction); drug-drug interactions.
    • Type III (orphan receptors) — function unknown; awaiting ligand identification.

5. Other Receptor Types

  • Adhesion receptors (integrins) — cell-cell & cell-matrix interactions; abciximab, eptifibatide, tirofiban (GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors); natalizumab (α4 integrin — MS); vedolizumab (α4β7 — IBD).
  • Soluble receptors (decoy receptors) — etanercept (TNF-α receptor-Fc fusion); anakinra (IL-1 receptor antagonist); canakinumab (anti-IL-1β).
  • Voltage-gated ion channels — not classical receptors but important drug targets — local anaesthetics (Na⁺ channel); CCBs (L-type Ca²⁺ channel); class I & IV antiarrhythmics; gabapentin, pregabalin (α2δ subunit of Ca²⁺ channel); sulfonylureas (KATP channel — SUR1 subunit).

Receptor Regulation (2 marks)

  • Down-regulation:
    • Prolonged agonist exposure → ↓ number of receptors (internalisation, degradation) → ↓ response (tolerance/tachyphylaxis).
    • Example — β2-agonists in asthma (salbutamol tolerance); opioids (tolerance); insulin resistance in type 2 diabetes.
  • Up-regulation:
    • Prolonged antagonist exposure or denervation → ↑ number of receptors → ↑ response on removal of antagonist (denervation supersensitivity).
    • Example — β-blocker withdrawal (overshoot hypertension); denervation of skeletal muscle (acetylcholine receptor up-regulation).
  • Desensitisation:
    • Rapid (seconds-minutes) — phosphorylation of receptor (PKA, PKC, GRK); β-arrestin binding; uncoupling from G-protein.
    • Slow (hours) — down-regulation (internalisation, degradation).
    • Receptor reserve / spare receptors:
      • Some tissues have more receptors than needed for maximal response — full agonist can produce maximal response by occupying only a fraction of receptors.
      • Important in pharmacology — partial agonist may appear as full agonist in tissues with receptor reserve.
      • Example — heart has β-receptor reserve; partial agonist pindolol may behave as full agonist.

    Clinical Pearl

    Receptor classification by transduction mechanism determines the speed & duration of drug action: ionotropic (milliseconds) for fast synaptic transmission (NMJ, anaesthesia); GPCR (seconds) for most neurotransmitters, hormones, autacoids; kinase-linked (minutes-hours) for growth factors, cytokines, insulin; intracellular/nuclear (hours-days) for steroids, thyroid hormone, vitamin D. Most therapeutic drugs target GPCRs (~30% of all marketed drugs) — adrenergic, muscarinic, histamine, serotonin, opioid, dopamine, angiotensin receptors. Receptor down-regulation explains tolerance — β2-agonists in asthma (need drug holiday); opioids (dose escalation); insulin resistance. Receptor up-regulation explains withdrawal phenomena — β-blocker withdrawal (overshoot hypertension, angina, MI); clonidine withdrawal (hypertensive crisis); always taper β-blockers & central α2-agonists. Steroid receptor pharmacology — glucocorticoids (anti-inflammatory), mineralocorticoids (aldosterone antagonists — spironolactone in heart failure, resistant hypertension); sex steroids (tamoxifen SERM in breast cancer; bicalutamide in prostate cancer). Targeted cancer therapy — kinase inhibitors revolutionised oncology — imatinib (CML — BCR-ABL), trastuzumab (breast cancer — HER2), erlotinib/gefitinib (NSCLC — EGFR), bevacizumab (VEGF); biomarker-driven therapy. Biologics (monoclonal antibodies, fusion proteins) target cytokines & cell-surface receptors — infliximab, adalimumab (TNF-α — RA, IBD); trastuzumab (HER2); rituximab (CD20); dupilumab (IL-4Rα — asthma, atopic dermatitis).

Introduction

Angina pectoris is the clinical syndrome of transient chest pain or discomfort due to myocardial ischaemia (imbalance between myocardial oxygen supply and demand). Three main types — stable (chronic stable) angina, unstable angina, variant (Prinzmetal/vasospastic) angina. Treatment aims to restore the supply-demand balance — reduce demand (heart rate, contractility, wall stress) and/or increase supply (coronary vasodilation).

Classification of Drugs Used in Angina Pectoris (5 marks)

A. Organic Nitrates

  • Short-acting — Nitroglycerin (glyceryl trinitrate, GTN) — sublingual tablet, spray; onset 1–3 min; duration 20–30 min.
  • Long-acting:
    • Isosorbide dinitrate (ISDN) — sublingual, oral; duration 4–6 h.
    • Isosorbide mononitrate (ISMN) — oral; duration 6–8 h.
    • Nitroglycerin transdermal patch, ointment — duration 8–14 h.
    • Erythrityl tetranitrate, pentaerythritol tetranitrate (rarely used).
    • Amyl nitrite (inhalant — historically for cyanide poisoning).

B. β-Adrenergic Blockers (β-Blockers)

  • Cardioselective (β1-selective) — Atenolol, Metoprolol, Bisoprolol, Nebivolol (also NO-mediated vasodilation), Acebutolol, Betaxolol, Esmolol (ultra-short-acting — IV).
  • Non-selective (β1 + β2) — Propranolol, Timolol, Nadolol, Sotalol (also class III antiarrhythmic).
  • Non-selective with α1-blockade — Carvedilol, Labetalol.

C. Calcium Channel Blockers (CCBs)

  • Dihydropyridines (DHP) — predominantly vasodilators:
    • Short-acting — Nifedipine (avoid short-acting capsule — reflex tachycardia, hypotension).
    • Long-acting — Amlodipine, Felodipine, Nicardipine, Lercanidipine, Nitrendipine, Clevidipine (IV).
  • Non-dihydropyridines (Non-DHP) — predominantly cardiac depressants:
    • Phenylalkylamine — Verapamil.
    • Benzothiazepine — Diltiazem.

D. Antiplatelet & Antithrombotic Drugs

  • Aspirin — COX-1 inhibitor; ↓platelet aggregation.
  • Clopidogrel, Prasugrel, Ticagrelor — P2Y12 ADP receptor antagonists.
  • Heparin, LMWH (enoxaparin), Fondaparinux — anticoagulants (acute coronary syndromes).
  • Abciximab, Eptifibatide, Tirofiban — GP IIb/IIIa antagonists (PCI).
  • Rivaroxaban, Apixaban — factor Xa inhibitors (recent ACS trials).

E. Lipid-Lowering Drugs

  • Statins — Atorvastatin, Rosuvastatin, Simvastatin, Pravastatin; HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors; plaque stabilisation; anti-inflammatory.
  • Ezetimibe — cholesterol absorption inhibitor.
  • PCSK9 inhibitors — Evolocumab, Alirocumab (familial hypercholesterolaemia, statin intolerance).
  • Bempedoic acid — ATP citrate lyase inhibitor.
  • Fibrates, Niacin, Omega-3 fatty acids — adjuncts.

F. Other Antianginal Drugs

  • Ranolazine — inhibits late sodium current (late INa) → ↓ Ca²⁺ overload → ↓ myocardial wall stress & oxygen demand; does not affect HR or BP; used for chronic stable angina refractory to standard therapy.
  • Ivabradine — selective inhibitor of If (funny channel) in SA node → ↓ heart rate without affecting contractility or BP; used for chronic stable angina in sinus rhythm with HR >70 bpm.
  • Nicorandil — nitrate + K-ATP channel opener; dual mechanism; vasodilator; used for stable angina.
  • Trimetazidine — inhibits fatty acid oxidation (3-ketoacyl-CoA thiolase) → shifts to glucose oxidation → ↓ oxygen demand; metabolic modulator.
  • Molsidomine — NO donor (like nitrates).
  • ACE inhibitors / ARBs — reduce CV events; protect endothelium; especially in diabetes, LV dysfunction, hypertension.

G. Combination Therapy

  • β-blocker + DHP-CCB (amlodipine) — synergistic; β-blocker counters reflex tachycardia from DHP.
  • β-blocker + long-acting nitrate.
  • Nitrate + CCB (avoid non-DHP + β-blocker — bradycardia, AV block).
  • Antiplatelet + statin + ACEI — for secondary prevention.

Mechanism of Action of Nitrates (5 marks)

1. Pharmacokinetics

  • Nitroglycerin (GTN):
    • Sublingual — onset 1–3 min; peak 4–8 min; duration 20–30 min; bioavailability <5% oral (extensive first-pass); sublingual bypasses liver.
    • IV — for unstable angina, acute MI, acute heart failure, hypertensive emergency; titratable.
    • Transdermal patch, ointment — sustained release; 8–14 h duration; patch-off period (12 h) to prevent tolerance.
    • Metabolism — by mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase-2 (ALDH2) in liver, blood vessel walls; inactive metabolites (glyceryl dinitrate, mononitrate, glycerol).
  • Isosorbide dinitrate (ISDN):
    • Sublingual — onset 2–5 min; duration 1–2 h.
    • Oral — onset 20–40 min; duration 4–6 h.
    • Hepatic metabolism to active ISMN (5-ISMN & 2-ISMN).
  • Isosorbide mononitrate (ISMN):
    • Oral — 100% bioavailability (no first-pass); duration 6–8 h.
    • Slow-release formulation — once daily; patch-off period (≥8 h) to prevent tolerance.

2. Mechanism of Action

  1. Prodrug activation:
    • Organic nitrates are prodrugs; require enzymatic bioactivation to release nitric oxide (NO).
    • ALDH2 (mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase-2) — main enzyme for nitroglycerin; converts GTN to 1,2-glyceryl dinitrate + nitrite → NO.
    • Other enzymes — cytochrome P450 reductase, xanthine oxidoreductase, glutathione-S-transferase.
    • Released NO is identical to endogenous endothelium-derived relaxing factor (EDRF) — discovered by Furchgott, Ignarro, Murad (Nobel Prize 1998).
  2. NO-mediated vasodilation:
    1. NO diffuses from endothelial cell (or from nitrate metabolism in vascular smooth muscle) to adjacent vascular smooth muscle cell.
    2. NO activates soluble guanylyl cyclase (sGC) → converts GTP → cyclic GMP (cGMP).
    3. cGMP activates protein kinase G (PKG).
    4. PKG phosphorylates multiple targets:
      • Phospholamban → ↑ Ca²⁺-ATPase (SERCA) → ↑ Ca²⁺ reuptake into sarcoplasmic reticulum → ↓ cytosolic Ca²⁺.
      • Myosin light chain phosphatase → dephosphorylates myosin light chain → relaxation.
      • K⁺ channels → hyperpolarisation → closes voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels → ↓ Ca²⁺ influx.
      • IP3 receptor → ↓ Ca²⁺ release.
    5. ↓ Intracellular Ca²⁺ → smooth muscle relaxation → vasodilation.
  3. Vascular selectivity:
    • Low doses — preferential venodilation (capacitance veins) → ↓ venous return (preload) → ↓ ventricular end-diastolic volume & wall stress → ↓ myocardial oxygen demand.
    • Higher doses — arteriolar dilation (resistance arteries) → ↓ peripheral resistance → ↓ afterload → ↓ myocardial work.
    • Coronary arteries:
      • Dilates large epicardial coronary arteries (conductance vessels) — improves blood flow to ischaemic subendocardium; redistributes flow.
      • Dilates collateral coronary vessels → improves perfusion of ischaemic areas.
      • Relieves coronary vasospasm (Prinzmetal angina).
      • Little effect on arterioles (<100 µm) — prevents "coronary steal" syndrome.
    • Platelets — NO + cGMP → ↓ platelet aggregation; may reduce thrombosis in unstable angina.

3. Haemodynamic Effects

  • Venodilation → ↓ preload (ventricular end-diastolic pressure & volume) → ↓ myocardial wall stress → ↓ oxygen demand.
  • Arteriolar dilation → ↓ afterload (systemic vascular resistance) → ↓ cardiac work → ↓ oxygen demand.
  • Coronary dilation → ↑ coronary blood flow; relief of spasm; redistribution to ischaemic subendocardium.
  • Reflex tachycardia — ↓ BP triggers baroreceptor reflex → ↑ sympathetic outflow → ↑ HR & contractility → may offset oxygen-sparing effect (combine with β-blocker).
  • Pulmonary vasodilation — ↓ pulmonary vascular resistance; useful in pulmonary oedema.
  • Reduced platelet aggregation — anti-thrombotic effect.

4. Therapeutic Uses

  • Acute anginal attack — sublingual GTN (1 tablet or spray under tongue; repeat every 5 min × 3 doses; if no relief, call emergency — possible MI).
  • Prophylaxis of stable angina — long-acting nitrates (ISMN, GTN patch) with patch-off period to prevent tolerance; β-blocker; CCB; aspirin; statin.
  • Variant (Prinzmetal) angina — nitrates + CCBs (especially DHP); avoid β-blockers (may worsen spasm via unopposed α).
  • Unstable angina / NSTEMI — IV nitroglycerin; antiplatelet (aspirin + clopidogrel/ticagrelor); anticoagulant (heparin/LMWH); statin; β-blocker; coronary angiography ± PCI.
  • Acute MI — IV nitroglycerin (if BP allows); aspirin; clopidogrel; heparin; β-blocker; ACEI; statin; primary PCI or thrombolysis.
  • Acute left ventricular failure / pulmonary oedema — IV/sublingual GTN; venodilation reduces preload; afterload reduction improves cardiac output.
  • Hypertensive emergency — IV nitroprusside (arterial + venous vasodilation); IV nitroglycerin (especially if cardiac ischaemia).
  • Chronic heart failure — ISDN + hydralazine (especially in African-Americans — A-HeFT trial with fixed-dose Bidil).
  • Anal fissure — topical GTN 0.2–0.4% ointment (relieves internal anal sphincter spasm).
  • Cyanide poisoning — sodium nitrite + sodium thiosulfate; amyl nitrite (forms methaemoglobin which binds cyanide).
  • Esophageal spasm, biliary colic — sublingual GTN may relieve smooth muscle spasm.

5. Adverse Effects

  • Vasodilatory:
    • Headache (most common; ~50%) — meningeal vasodilation; ameliorates with continued use; treat with paracetamol.
    • Flushing, dizziness, postural hypotension, syncope.
    • Reflex tachycardia — may worsen angina; combine with β-blocker.
  • Methaemoglobinaemia — high doses or prolonged use; nitrites oxidise Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ in haemoglobin; ↓ oxygen-carrying capacity; treat with methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg IV.
  • Tolerance (nitrate tolerance) — develops with continuous therapy (>24 h); due to:
    • Depletion of sulphydryl (-SH) groups (required for ALDH2-mediated NO release) — "thiol hypothesis".
    • ↑ ALDH2 inactivation by oxidative stress.
    • ↑ Superoxide production → ↑ NO degradation (uncoupling of eNOS).
    • Neurohormonal activation — RAAS, sympathetic activation.
    • Plasma volume expansion.
  • Prevention — nitrate-free interval (≥8–12 h daily); eccentric dosing (e.g., ISMN at 8 AM & 2 PM — nitrate-free overnight); intermittent transdermal patch (12 h on, 12 h off).
  • Withdrawal / rebound — abrupt cessation of long-term nitrate therapy → rebound vasoconstriction, angina, MI; taper gradually.
  • Alcohol interaction — severe hypotension; avoid concurrent use.
  • Sildenafil (PDE5 inhibitor) interaction — contraindicated; both ↑ cGMP → severe, life-threatening hypotension; at least 24 h gap (48 h for tadalafil).
  • Increased intracranial pressure — vasodilation; avoid in raised ICP, recent head injury.
  • Increased intraocular pressure — historical concern (open-angle glaucoma); modern evidence suggests safe.
  • Contact dermatitis — transdermal patch.
  • Sodium nitroprusside — cyanide & thiocyanate toxicity (with prolonged use >48 h or renal impairment); monitor thiocyanate levels; treat with sodium thiosulfate + hydroxocobalamin.

6. Contraindications

  • Hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg).
  • Severe aortic stenosis, hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM) — ↓ preload worsens outflow obstruction.
  • Right ventricular infarction — ↓ preload worsens RV failure.
  • Recent PDE5 inhibitor use (sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil) — within 24–48 h.
  • Severe anaemia (methaemoglobinaemia risk).
  • Raised intracranial pressure (head injury, haemorrhage).
  • Hypersensitivity to nitrates.
  • Constrictive pericarditis, cardiac tamponade.

Nitrates remain first-line for acute angina relief — sublingual GTN tablet or spray under tongue; relief within 1–3 min; if no relief after 3 doses 5 min apart, call emergency — possible MI. Introduction

Adrenergic transmission refers to the synthesis, storage, release, action, and termination of the neurotransmitter noradrenaline (norepinephrine) at sympathetic postganglionic nerve terminals (and adrenaline from adrenal medulla). Understanding this process is essential for pharmacology of sympathomimetics, sympatholytics, and many cardiovascular drugs.

Steps of Adrenergic Transmission (6 marks)

Step 1 — Synthesis of Noradrenaline

Occurs in the neuronal cytoplasm; catalysed by three enzymes acting sequentially:

  1. Tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) — rate-limiting step; converts L-tyrosine → L-DOPA (3,4-dihydroxyphenylalanine); requires tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4), Fe²⁺, O₂; feedback-inhibited by noradrenaline (end-product inhibition).
  2. DOPA decarboxylase (aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase, AADC) — converts L-DOPA → dopamine; requires pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6).
  3. Dopamine β-hydroxylase (DβH) — converts dopamine → noradrenaline; requires ascorbic acid (vitamin C), Cu²⁺, O₂; located in vesicle (after dopamine enters vesicle).
  4. In adrenal medulla, additional enzyme phenylethanolamine-N-methyltransferase (PNMT) — converts noradrenaline → adrenaline; requires S-adenosylmethionine (SAM); located in cytoplasm (adrenaline then re-enters vesicle).

Step 2 — Storage in Vesicles

  • Dopamine (cytoplasmic) is taken up into synaptic vesicles (dense-core granules) via vesicular monoamine transporter (VMAT2) — H⁺-ATPase-driven, exchange H⁺ for monoamine; blocked by reserpine & tetrabenazine.
  • Inside vesicle, DβH converts dopamine → noradrenaline.
  • Noradrenaline stored with ATP (4:1 molar ratio), chromogranin A, DβH, enkephalins; forms dense core.
  • Vesicular storage protects noradrenaline from degradation by MAO (mitochondrial).

Step 3 — Release

  • Action potential arrives at varicosity → opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels (N-type, P/Q-type) → Ca²⁺ influx.
  • ↑ Ca²⁺ triggers vesicle docking (SNARE complex — synaptobrevin, SNAP-25, syntaxin) & fusion with plasma membrane.
  • Exocytosis — noradrenaline + ATP + DβH + chromogranin released into synaptic cleft.
  • Modulation of release:
    • α2-presynaptic autoinhibitory receptors — noradrenaline binds α2 on its own neuron → ↓ Ca²⁺ influx → ↓ further release (negative feedback); blocked by α2 antagonists (yohimbine, phentolamine) → ↑ release.
    • β2-presynaptic facilitatory receptors — adrenaline enhances release (positive feedback).
    • Presynaptic receptors for other transmitters:
      • M2 muscarinic (acetylcholine) — inhibits release.
      • H2 histamine, A2 adenosine, PGE2, GABA-B, opioids, somatostatin — inhibit.
      • Angiotensin II (AT1), 5-HT2 — facilitate.

Step 4 — Receptor Action

Noradrenaline binds to adrenergic receptors on postsynaptic (and presynaptic) cells:

  • α1 (Gq) — vasoconstriction (skin, splanchnic), mydriasis, piloerection, ejaculation, bladder neck contraction, GI sphincter contraction; IP3/DAG/PKC → ↑ intracellular Ca²⁺.
  • α2 (Gi) — presynaptic inhibition of noradrenaline release; platelet aggregation; insulin inhibition; ↓ cAMP.
  • β1 (Gs) — ↑ heart rate (SA node), ↑ contractility (atria, ventricles), ↑ AV conduction, ↑ renin release (kidney); ↑ cAMP → PKA.
  • β2 (Gs) — bronchodilation, vasodilation (skeletal muscle), uterine relaxation (tocolysis), glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, ↑ insulin release, mast cell stabilisation.
  • β3 (Gs) — lipolysis (adipose); thermogenesis; bladder detrusor relaxation (mirabegron).

Step 5 — Termination of Action

Two mechanisms:

  1. Neuronal reuptake (Uptake-1) — primary mechanism (~80%); noradrenaline taken back into nerve terminal via norepinephrine transporter (NET, uptake-1) — Na⁺/Cl⁻-dependent, high affinity, saturable; also takes up adrenaline, dopamine, tyramine, amphetamine, metaraminol. Then re-stored in vesicles (via VMAT2) or degraded by MAO.
  2. Extraneuronal uptake (Uptake-2) — non-neuronal; into effector cells (smooth muscle, glial, liver) via extraneuronal monoamine transporter (EMT, uptake-2) — low affinity, high capacity; adrenaline, isoprenaline preferred; followed by degradation by COMT.
  3. Diffusion — small amount enters systemic circulation; reaches liver (COMT, MAO).

Step 6 — Metabolism

Two enzymes degrade catecholamines:

  • Monoamine oxidase (MAO):
    • Mitochondrial; located in neurons (MAO-A), glial cells, liver, GI tract.
    • MAO-A — deaminates noradrenaline, adrenaline, serotonin (5-HT); inhibited by moclobemide (selective MAO-A inhibitor).
    • MAO-B — deaminates dopamine, phenylethylamine; inhibited by selegiline, rasagiline (Parkinson's disease).
    • Converts noradrenaline → 3,4-dihydroxymandelic acid (DOMA) → vanillylmandelic acid (VMA).
  • Catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT):
    • Cytosolic; located in synaptic cleft, effector cells, liver, kidney; not in neurons.
    • Catalyses O-methylation of catecholamines; requires Mg²⁺, S-adenosylmethionine (SAM).
    • Converts noradrenaline → normetanephrine; adrenaline → metanephrine; dopamine → 3-methoxytyramine.
    • Inhibited by entacapone, tolcapone (Parkinson's disease — prolong L-DOPA action).
  • Final metabolites:
    • Noradrenaline → 3-methoxy-4-hydroxymandelic acid (VMA — vanillylmandelic acid) — main urinary metabolite.
    • Adrenaline → metanephrine → VMA.
    • Dopamine → homovanillic acid (HVA).
  • Clinical use — VMA (24-hour urine) & plasma/urinary metanephrines for diagnosis of phaeochromocytoma; HVA for neuroblastoma.

Drugs Acting Through Modification of Adrenergic Transmission (9 marks)

A. Drugs Affecting Synthesis

  • α-Methyl-p-tyrosine (metyrosine) — inhibits tyrosine hydroxylase (rate-limiting step); ↓ synthesis of catecholamines; used for phaeochromocytoma (pre-operative), refractory hypertension.
  • Carbidopa, benserazide — peripheral DOPA decarboxylase inhibitors; do not cross BBB; combined with levodopa in Parkinson's disease — ↑ brain delivery of L-DOPA, ↓ peripheral side effects (nausea, arrhythmia).
  • α-Methyldopa — false neurotransmitter precursor; converted to α-methyl-noradrenaline (less potent vasoconstrictor than noradrenaline) → replaces noradrenaline in vesicles → released → acts on central α2 receptors (in medulla) → ↓ sympathetic outflow → antihypertensive; used in pregnancy-induced hypertension.
  • Disulfiram — inhibits DβH (also aldehyde dehydrogenase) → ↓ noradrenaline synthesis; historical (not used clinically for this purpose).

B. Drugs Affecting Storage

  • Reserpine — irreversible inhibitor of VMAT2 → noradrenaline leaks into cytoplasm → degraded by MAO → depletion of vesicular noradrenaline; antihypertensive (rarely used now; side effects — severe depression, parkinsonism, peptic ulcer, diarrhoea).
  • Tetrabenazine — reversible VMAT2 inhibitor; depletes central monoamines (dopamine > noradrenaline > serotonin); used for Huntington's chorea, tardive dyskinesia.
  • 6-Hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA) — neurotoxin; taken up by noradrenergic neurons → destroys them; experimental.

C. Drugs Affecting Release

  • Indirectly acting sympathomimetics — taken up by NET (uptake-1) into neuron → displace noradrenaline from vesicles → noradrenaline released into synaptic cleft → acts on receptors:
    • Amphetamine, methamphetamine — CNS stimulants (release dopamine & noradrenaline); ADHD, narcolepsy; abuse potential.
    • Ephedrine, pseudoephedrine — mixed action (direct + indirect); nasal decongestant; ephedrine for hypotension (anaesthesia).
    • Phenylpropanolamine — nasal decongestant; withdrawn (haemorrhagic stroke risk).
    • Tyramine — in fermented foods (cheese, wine, beer); normally metabolised by MAO in gut & liver; in patients on MAO inhibitors → reaches sympathetic nerve terminals → displaces noradrenaline → hypertensive crisis ("cheese reaction").
    • Metaraminol — indirect + direct α-agonist; shock.
  • α2-Agonists (centrally acting):
    • Clonidine — central α2 agonist (brainstem) → ↓ sympathetic outflow → ↓ BP, HR; also ↓ renal renin; antihypertensive; ADHD (patch), opioid/alcohol withdrawal, severe pain.
    • α-Methyldopa — prodrug; converted to α-methylnoradrenaline → central α2 agonist; antihypertensive; pregnancy.
    • Guanfacine, guanabenz — α2A-selective; ADHD (guanfacine); hypertension.
    • Dexmedetomidine — α2A-selective; IV sedative in ICU; analgesia; anxiolysis; minimal respiratory depression.
    • Tizanidine — α2 agonist; centrally acting skeletal muscle relaxant (spasticity, multiple sclerosis).
    • Brimonidine, apraclonidine — α2 agonist; glaucoma (↓ aqueous humour production); brimonidine also reduces redness.
  • α2-Antagonists:
    • Yohimbine, rauwolscine — α2 antagonist; ↑ noradrenaline release; experimental; used for psychogenic erectile dysfunction; anxiety.
    • Mirtazapine — α2 antagonist (also 5-HT2/5-HT3 antagonist); antidepressant; ↑ noradrenaline & serotonin release.
  • Bretylium — blocks noradrenaline release (taken up by NET, accumulates in neuron, blocks Ca²⁺-dependent release); class III antiarrhythmic (historical — VT/VF).
  • Guanethidine — taken up by NET → displaces noradrenaline → depletes stores → blocks release; antihypertensive (historical; rarely used).
  • Botulinum toxin — blocks SNARE complex → prevents exocytosis; used for cervical dystonia, spasticity, wrinkles, migraine, hyperhidrosis, strabismus; (cholinergic junctions more affected than adrenergic).

D. Drugs Affecting Reuptake (NET Inhibitors)

  • Cocaine — blocks NET (and DAT, SERT) → ↑ noradrenaline, dopamine, serotonin in synapse → CNS stimulation, euphoria, vasoconstriction, hypertension; local anaesthetic (topical); high abuse potential.
  • Tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) — amitriptyline, imipramine, nortriptyline, desipramine — inhibit NET & SERT → ↑ noradrenaline & serotonin; antidepressant, neuropathic pain, migraine prophylaxis, enuresis.
  • Atomoxetine — selective NET inhibitor; ADHD (non-stimulant).
  • Reboxetine — selective NRI; antidepressant (Europe).
  • Viloxazine — NRI; ADHD.
  • SNRIs — venlafaxine, duloxetine, desvenlafaxine, milnacipran, levomilnacipran — inhibit SERT & NET; depression, anxiety, neuropathic pain, fibromyalgia.
  • Nortriptyline, desipramine — more NRI than SRI.

E. Drugs Affecting Metabolism

  • MAO inhibitors (MAOIs):
    • Non-selective (MAO-A + B) — phenelzine, tranylcypromine, isocarboxazid; antidepressants; risk of cheese reaction (tyramine); hypertensive crisis with SSRIs, meperidine ("serotonin syndrome").
    • MAO-A selective (RIMA) — moclobemide; antidepressant; less risk of cheese reaction.
    • MAO-B selective — selegiline (L-deprenyl), rasagiline; Parkinson's disease (↓ dopamine degradation; enhances L-DOPA effect); low risk of cheese reaction at low doses; selegiline at high doses loses selectivity.
    • Linezolid — antibiotic; weak non-selective MAOI; risk of serotonin syndrome with SSRIs.
    • Methylene blue — MAOI; risk with SSRIs.
    • Procarbazine — anticancer; weak MAOI.
  • COMT inhibitors:

  • α2-agonists — clonidine, methyldopa, dexmedetomidine, brimonidine (see above).

Definition

Anticoagulants are drugs that prevent or reduce the coagulation (clotting) of blood — used in prevention & treatment of thromboembolic disorders (DVT, PE, atrial fibrillation, mechanical heart valves, ACS).

Classification of Anticoagulants (3 marks)

A. Parenteral Anticoagulants

  1. Indirect thrombin inhibitors (acting via antithrombin):
    • Heparin (Unfractionated Heparin, UFH) — IV/SC; inhibits thrombin (IIa) & factor Xa via antithrombin (AT).
    • Low Molecular Weight Heparin (LMWH) — enoxaparin, dalteparin, tinzaparin; SC; preferentially inhibit factor Xa > thrombin.
    • Fondaparinux — synthetic pentasaccharide; selective factor Xa inhibitor via antithrombin; SC.
    • Idraparinux, idrabiotaparinux — long-acting pentasaccharides (investigational).
  2. Direct thrombin inhibitors (do not require antithrombin):
    • Lepirudin, desirudin — recombinant hirudin (from leech); IV/SC; for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT).
    • Bivalirudin — hirudin analogue; IV; PCI, HIT.
    • Argatroban — small molecule; IV; HIT.

B. Oral Anticoagulants

  1. Vitamin K Antagonists (Coumarins):
    • Warfarin — most common; racemic mixture.
    • A cenocoumarol — shorter half-life; used in Europe, India.
    • Phenprocoumon — longer half-life; Europe.
    • Dicoumarol, ethyl biscoumacetate — historical.
  2. Direct Oral Anticoagulants (DOACs / NOACs / Target-Specific Oral Anticoagulants):
    • Direct thrombin (IIa) inhibitor — Dabigatran (Pradaxa).
    • Direct factor Xa inhibitors:
      • Rivaroxaban (Xarelto).
      • Apixaban (Eliquis).
      • Edoxaban (Lixiana, Savaysa).
      • Betrixaban (Bevyxxa) — withdrawn.

C. Other Anticoagulants

  • Defibrotide — purified polydeoxyribonucleotide; modulates endothelial function; hepatic veno-occlusive disease (VOD) post-HSCT.
  • Antithrombin concentrate — for AT deficiency; heparin resistance.
  • Protein C concentrate — purpura fulminans (homozygous protein C deficiency).
  • Thrombomodulin (recombinant soluble) — sepsis-associated DIC (historical).
  • Sulodexide — glycosaminoglycan; diabetic nephropathy (investigational).

Heparin (5 marks)

Source & Chemistry

  • Naturally occurring glycosaminoglycan (mucopolysaccharide); extracted from porcine intestinal mucosa or bovine lung.
  • Mixture of sulphated polysaccharides; MW 3,000–30,000 Da (average 15,000).
  • Strongly negatively charged (sulphate groups) — basis for neutralisation by protamine sulphate (positively charged).

Mechanism of Action

  1. Heparin binds to antithrombin III (AT) (endogenous serine protease inhibitor) via a specific pentasaccharide sequence.
  2. Binding induces conformational change in AT → exposes active site → accelerates AT-mediated inhibition of clotting factors (1000-fold).
  3. Inactivates thrombin (IIa), factor Xa, IXa, XIa, XIIa, kallikrein.
  4. Unfractionated heparin inhibits both thrombin & factor Xa equally (1:1 ratio).
  5. LMWH (<6500 Da) — preferentially inhibits factor Xa (ratio ~3–4:1) — cannot simultaneously bind thrombin & AT (short chain).
  6. Fondaparinux — pure pentasaccharide; exclusively inhibits factor Xa.

Pharmacokinetics

  • Not absorbed orally (large, charged molecule); given IV or SC.
  • Onset — IV immediate; SC 1–2 h.
  • Half-life — 1–2 h (dose-dependent; longer at high doses); 60–90 min after IV bolus.
  • Metabolism — hepatic (heparinase) & reticuloendothelial; partial renal excretion.
  • Does not cross placenta (large molecule) — safe in pregnancy.
  • Monitoring — aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time); target 1.5–2.5× control. LMWH does not require routine monitoring (predictable pharmacokinetics); monitor anti-Xa level in pregnancy, renal impairment, obesity, children.
  • Antidote — protamine sulphate 1 mg neutralises 100 U heparin (given IV slowly; risk of hypotension, anaphylaxis).

Therapeutic Uses

  • Venous thromboembolism (VTE) — DVT & PE — acute & long-term.
  • Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) — unstable angina, NSTEMI, STEMI (with antiplatelets).
  • PCI (percutaneous coronary intervention) — UFH or bivalirudin.
  • Atrial fibrillation — cardioversion (if not on warfarin/DOAC); bridging therapy.
  • Mechanical heart valves — perioperative bridging.
  • Cardiopulmonary bypass, haemodialysis, extracorporeal circuits — anticoagulation.
  • Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) — selected cases (with bleeding).
  • Pregnancy — LMWH for VTE prophylaxis/treatment, mechanical heart valves, antiphospholipid syndrome (APS).
  • Heparin flushes — IV catheter patency.

Adverse Effects

  • Bleeding — most common; dose-dependent; monitor aPTT; reverse with protamine.
  • Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT):
    • Immune-mediated (IgG antibody against heparin-platelet factor 4 [PF4] complex).
    • Type I — mild, non-immune, early (days 1–4), platelet count >100,000; not clinically significant.
    • Type II — severe, immune-mediated, 5–14 days after exposure (or sooner if previous exposure); platelet count <100,000 (or 50% drop); paradoxical thrombosis (arterial & venous) — limb gangrene, stroke, PE; STOP heparin immediately; switch to direct thrombin inhibitor (argatroban, bivalirudin) or fondaparinux; never re-expose to heparin.

  • Priapism — rare.

  • Active bleeding (GI, intracranial, etc.).
  • Severe bleeding diathesis (haemophilia, thrombocytopenia <50,000).
  • Recent neurosurgery, ophthalmic surgery, intracranial haemorrhage.
  • Severe uncontrolled hypertension.
  • Bacterial endocarditis (risk of mycotic aneurysm rupture).
  • HIT (current or past).
  • Known hypersensitivity (porcine or bovine).

Source & Chemistry

  • 4-Hydroxycoumarin derivative; synthetic; racemic mixture of R- & S-enantiomers (S more potent).
  • Discovered as cause of haemorrhagic disease in cattle (sweet clover disease — dicoumarol from spoiled sweet clover; Link, 1940s); warfarin developed as rat poison (1948); first used clinically in 1954.
  • Oral; highly protein-bound (99%); small volume of distribution.

Mechanism of Action

  1. Inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1) — enzyme that recycles oxidised vitamin K (vitamin K 2,3-epoxide) back to active reduced form (hydroquinone, KH2).
  2. ↓ Active vitamin K → ↓ γ-carboxylation of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors.
  3. Vitamin K-dependent clotting factors — II (prothrombin), VII, IX, X; also protein C & protein S (endogenous anticoagulants).
  4. γ-carboxylation (by γ-glutamyl carboxylase) adds carboxyl groups to glutamic acid residues → γ-carboxyglutamic acid (GLA) → enables calcium binding → anchors factors to phospholipid surfaces → active clotting.
  5. Without γ-carboxylation, factors are dysfunctional (PIVKA — Proteins Induced by Vitamin K Antagonism).
  6. Onset of action — slow (8–12 h for factor VII; 2–7 days for full anticoagulation) — due to long half-life of existing carboxylated factors (II: 60 h, X: 24–48 h, VII: 6 h, IX: 24 h).
  7. Protein C has shortest half-life (8 h) — its levels fall first → transient procoagulant state → skin necrosis in deficient patients.

  • Rapid & complete oral absorption; bioavailability ~100%.
  • 99% bound to plasma albumin; small Vd (~0.14 L/kg).
  • Hepatic metabolism — CYP2C9 (S-warfarin, more potent); CYP1A2, CYP3A4 (R-warfarin).
  • Half-life — 36–42 h; long duration of action.
  • Crosses placenta — teratogenic (contraindicated in pregnancy).
  • Monitoring — PT (Prothrombin Time) / INR (International Normalised Ratio).

  • Antidote — vitamin K1 (phytonadione) (oral, SC, IV — slow); FFP (fresh frozen plasma); PCC (prothrombin complex concentrate — four-factor preferred); recombinant factor VIIa (refractory).

  • VTE (DVT & PE) — treatment & secondary prevention — 3–6 months (provoked) or lifelong (unprovoked, recurrent, cancer, thrombophilia).
  • Atrial fibrillation — stroke prevention (CHA2DS2-VASc score ≥2 in men, ≥3 in women).

    • Higher risk in protein C deficiency (congenital or acquired).
    • Prevention — "bridge" with heparin (UFH/LMWH) until INR therapeutic for 2 days; start warfarin at low dose (2.5–5 mg); check protein C level if family history.
    • Treatment — stop warfarin; give vitamin K; heparin; FFP/PCC; protein C concentrate if deficient.
  • Teratogenicity:
    • Contraindicated in pregnancy (crosses placenta).
    • 1st trimester — embryopathy (nasal hypoplasia, stippled epiphyses, limb hypoplasia, ocular abnormalities); "warfarin embryopathy" — risk 5–10% if exposed weeks 6–12.
    • 2nd & 3rd trimester — foetal bleeding, CNS abnormalities (Dandy-Walker malformation, optic atrophy), miscarriage, stillbirth.
    • Use LMWH in pregnancy; switch back to warfarin postpartum (safe in breastfeeding).
  • Purple toe syndrome — rare; cholesterol microembolisation; painful purple toes; stop warfarin.

    • Decreased vitamin K absorption — antibiotics (kill gut flora that synthesise vitamin K2); cholestyramine, orlistat, mineral oil.
    • ↑ Catabolism of clotting factors — thyroid hormones.
    • Additive bleeding risk — antiplatelets (aspirin, clopidogrel), NSAIDs, SSRIs.
    • Alcohol — acutely inhibits metabolism (↑ INR); chronically induces enzymes (↓ INR).
  • Reduced anticoagulation (↓ INR, thrombosis risk):
    • CYP inducers — rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital, griseofulvin, St John's wort, nevirapine.
    • ↑ Vitamin K intake — green leafy vegetables, supplements, enteral feeds.
    • Reduced absorption — cholestyramine, sucralfate, antacids.

Advantages over warfarin

  • Predictable pharmacokinetics — no routine monitoring (no INR).
  • Rapid onset (2–4 h) — no heparin bridging.
  • Short half-life — quick offset.
  • Few drug interactions (CYP3A4/P-gp).
  • No dietary vitamin K restriction.
  • Lower intracranial haemorrhage risk than warfarin (in AF trials).

Disadvantages

  • Renal excretion — dose adjustment in CKD; avoid in severe renal impairment (CrCl <30 for dabigatran, <15 for rivaroxaban/apixaban).
  • Cost — expensive vs warfarin.
  • No routine monitoring — compliance concern.
  • Antidotes expensive & not always available.
  • Higher GI bleeding risk than warfarin (especially dabigatran, rivaroxaban).
  • Not recommended in pregnancy, mechanical heart valves (RE-ALIGN trial — dabigatran worse than warfarin).
  • Antiphospholipid syndrome with triple positivity — warfarin preferred.

Clinical Pearl

Heparin & warfarin have different mechanisms — heparin potentiates antithrombin (immediate); warfarin inhibits vitamin K recycling (slow onset, days). Always bridge with heparin when starting warfarin — 5–7 days overlap until INR therapeutic for 2 consecutive days, then stop heparin. Warfarin skin necrosis — occurs in first week; due to protein C depletion (shortest half-life) before procoagulant factors fall → transient procoagulant state; higher risk in protein C deficiency; prevent with heparin bridging & low starting dose. HIT (heparin-induced thrombocytopenia) type II — paradoxical thrombosis 5–14 days after heparin; platelet count drops >50%; STOP all heparin immediately; switch to argatroban or bivalirudin (direct thrombin inhibitors); never re-expose to heparin/LMWH. Warfarin is teratogenic — avoid in pregnancy; use LMWH (does not cross placenta). Always check INR before surgery/procedure — stop warfarin 5 days before; bridge with LMWH if high thrombotic risk (mechanical valve, recent VTE, AF with high CHA2DS2-VASc). DOACs are replacing warfarin for most indications (AF, VTE) — no monitoring, no dietary restriction, fewer interactions, lower intracranial bleed. However, warfarin remains preferred for — mechanical heart valves, severe renal impairment, antiphospholipid syndrome (triple positive), pregnancy (LMWH preferred actually), patients with poor adherence (warfarin's long half-life is forgiving). Reversal — warfarin: vitamin K + FFP or PCC (4-factor preferred); heparin: protamine; dabigatran: idarucizumab; rivaroxaban/apixaban: andexanet alfa; all: supportive care, activated charcoal if recent ingestion. India — warfarin widely used (low cost); DOACs increasingly available but expensive; generic apixaban launched 2023 — improving affordability.

Clinical Approach to the Unconscious Patient — Suspected Poisoning

The 35-year-old male brought unconscious to the emergency requires a systematic ABCDE approach with simultaneous history taking, examination, investigations, and empirical treatment. Common causes of unconsciousness in a young adult include poisoning (organophosphorus, opioid, benzodiazepine, alcohol, carbon monoxide, barbiturate, tricyclic antidepressant), head trauma, metabolic (hypoglycaemia, DKA, hepatic encephalopathy), CNS infection, post-ictal state, and stroke.

Step 1 — Initial Assessment & Resuscitation (ABCDE) (3 marks)

  1. Airway (A) — assess patency; clear secretions, vomitus; head tilt-chin lift or jaw thrust (if cervical spine injury suspected); oropharyngeal/nasopharyngeal airway; endotracheal intubation if GCS <8, absent gag reflex, or unable to maintain airway.
  2. Breathing (B) — assess rate, depth, pattern, chest movement, SpO₂; oxygen 100% via mask (15 L/min with non-rebreather mask); bag-mask ventilation if apnoeic; mechanical ventilation if respiratory failure; check for cyanosis, needle decompression if tension pneumothorax.
  3. Circulation (C) — assess pulse, BP, heart rate, capillary refill, skin temperature; IV access (2 large-bore cannulae); fluid bolus (normal saline 20 mL/kg) if hypotensive; ECG monitoring; treat arrhythmias; check blood glucose (hypoglycaemia — give 50 mL 50% dextrose IV after taking blood sample); vasopressors (noradrenaline) if refractory shock.
  4. Disability (D) — GCS (Glasgow Coma Scale); pupil size & reactivity (pinpoint — opioid, organophosphorus; dilated — TCA, atropine, antihistamine); check for focal neurological deficits, meningismus, trauma signs; blood glucose; AVPU.
  5. Exposure (E) — fully expose patient; look for evidence of poisoning (injection marks, pill bottles, suicide note, chemical smell — garlic [organophosphorus, arsenic], bitter almond [cyanide], rotten eggs [H2S]); check skin for tracks, burns, petechiae; rectal temperature.

Step 2 — Rapid History (from relatives, bystanders, paramedics) (1 mark)

  • What was the patient doing before collapse? — work (agriculture — organophosphorus), home, social.
  • Any chemicals/medications found nearby? — empty bottles, blister packs, syringes.
  • Time of exposure — determines decontamination strategy.
  • Route of exposure — ingestion, inhalation, injection, dermal.
  • Past medical history — depression, diabetes, epilepsy, cardiac disease, addiction.
  • Current medications — especially insulin, oral hypoglycaemics, opioids, TCAs, lithium.
  • Occupational exposure — farmer (OPC), factory worker, painter.
  • Recent stressors — financial, relationship, exam.
  • Witnessed seizure, trauma, fever before collapse.
