Step 4 — Investigations (2 marks)

  • Bedside:
    • Blood glucose — hypoglycaemia (insulin, sulfonylurea, alcohol) → give dextrose.
    • ECG — arrhythmia, QT prolongation (TCAs, antipsychotics, erythromycin), QRS widening (TCAs, sodium channel blockers).
    • Pulse oximetry — CO poisoning may have normal SpO₂ (use CO-oximetry).
    • ABG — metabolic acidosis (methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylates, TCAs); respiratory acidosis (opioids, sedatives).
  • Laboratory:
    • CBG — leucocytosis; anaemia; thrombocytopenia.
    • Electrolytes, urea, creatinine — renal failure; anion gap (methanol, ethylene glycol).
    • LFT — hepatic failure (paracetamol, mushroom poisoning).
    • CK — rhabdomyolysis (prolonged immobilisation, NMS, serotonin syndrome, statins).
    • Coagulation — DIC; warfarin overdose.
    • Plasma cholinesterase & RBC acetylcholinesterase — organophosphorus poisoning.
    • Drug levels — paracetamol (4-hour level — Rumack-Matthew nomogram), salicylate, lithium, digoxin, iron, methanol (osmolal gap), ethylene glycol (osmolal gap + crystals in urine), theophylline, valproate, phenytoin, carbamazepine.
    • Urine drug screen — opioids, amphetamines, cocaine, cannabis, benzodiazepines, barbiturates.
  • Imaging:
    • Chest X-ray — aspiration pneumonia, pulmonary oedema (opioids, salicylates), chemical pneumonitis (hydrocarbons).
    • CT head — exclude intracranial haemorrhage, mass, trauma; especially if focal signs or no improvement.

Step 5 — General Management of Poisoning (4 marks)

A. Decontamination

  • Activated charcoal (single dose):
    • 1 g/kg (adults 50–100 g) within 1 h of ingestion; adsorbs drugs in gut.
    • Effective for most oral poisons except — alcohols, hydrocarbons, metals (iron, lithium, potassium), strong acids/alkalis, cyanide.
    • Contraindicated — unprotected airway (aspiration risk), corrosive ingestion, ileus, GI obstruction.
  • Gastric lavage:
    • Rarely used now — only if life-threatening ingestion within 1 h & airway protected.
    • Contraindicated — corrosives, hydrocarbons (aspiration risk), unknown time of ingestion.
  • Whole bowel irrigation — polyethylene glycol electrolyte solution; for sustained-release drugs, iron, lithium, packets of illicit drugs (body packers).
  • Syrup of ipecac — no longer recommended.
  • Skin decontamination — remove clothes; wash with soap & water (organophosphorus); staff protection.
  • Eye decontamination — copious saline irrigation for 15–30 min.

B. Enhanced Elimination

  • Multiple-dose activated charcoal (MDAC) — 25 g every 4 h; interrupts enterohepatic circulation; for carbamazepine, dapsone, phenobarbital, quinine, theophylline, salicylates.
  • Urinary alkalinisation — IV sodium bicarbonate to maintain urine pH >7.5; enhances excretion of weak acids (salicylates, phenobarbital, methotrexate).
  • Haemodialysis:
    • For small, water-soluble, low protein-bound, low Vd drugs — methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylates, lithium, metformin, theophylline, valproate, carbamazepine (severe).
    • Indications — severe acidosis, renal failure, haemodynamic instability, very high drug levels, end-organ toxicity.
  • Haemoperfusion — charcoal column; theophylline, barbiturates; rarely used now.

Step 6 — Supportive Care & Disposition (2 marks)

  • ICU admission for — coma (GCS <8), respiratory failure, cardiac instability, seizures, severe metabolic derangement, need for antidote infusion.
  • Continuous monitoring — ECG, BP, SpO₂, urine output, neurology.
  • Treat complications — aspiration pneumonia (antibiotics), pressure sores (turning), DVT prophylaxis (LMWH — if no bleeding), rhabdomyolysis (IV fluids, alkalinise urine), renal failure (haemodialysis), hepatic failure (NAC for paracetamol, supportive).
  • Psychiatric evaluation — once conscious; rule out suicidal intent; admit under Mental Healthcare Act if necessary.
  • Forensic / medico-legal documentation — preserve samples (blood, urine, gastric contents) for forensic analysis; police intimation if unnatural cause suspected.
  • Discharge planning — psychiatric follow-up; family counselling; poison prevention education.

Clinical Pearl

Always check blood glucose first in any unconscious patient — hypoglycaemia is the most easily reversible cause and missed diagnosis can be devastating. Empirical "coma cocktail" — naloxone (opioid), dextrose (hypoglycaemia), thiamine (alcoholic — Wernicke's encephalopathy). Pupil examination is the single most useful bedside sign — pinpoint (opioid, organophosphorus); dilated (anticholinergic, TCA, sympathomimetic); normal (sedative-hypnotic). Always suspect organophosphorus poisoning in Indian agricultural workers — miosis, salivation, lacrimation, fasciculations, bradycardia, bronchospasm (SLUDGE-BB); give atropine (titrate to atropinisation) + pralidoxime (2-PAM) ASAP; check plasma cholinesterase. Paracetamol poisoning — silent for 24 h, then hepatic failure; check 4-hour plasma level against Rumack-Matthew nomogram; N-acetylcysteine is antidote (most effective within 8 h, but give up to 24 h or beyond if liver injury). Tricyclic antidepressant overdose — QRS >100 ms is danger sign; treat with sodium bicarbonate (alkalinise plasma to pH 7.45–7.55); avoid class Ia, Ic antiarrhythmics; flumazenil contraindicated (seizure risk). Always involve poison control centre for advice; document all interventions; medico-legal samples preserved. India — common poisonings — organophosphorus (farmers), aluminium phosphide (fumigant — "rice tablet"; fatal — no antidote; magnesium sulphate may help), oleander seeds, snake bite, benzodiazepines, alcohol, paracetamol, pesticides (endosulfan, paraquat). Prevention — restrict access to pesticides; safe storage; community education; mental health support; pesticide regulation.
